intro:
2 Kings picks up right where 1 Kings ended—Elijah's ministry concluding, Elisha's beginning. Elijah knows his departure time. He asks Elisha 'What can I do for you before I'm taken?' Elisha: 'Double portion of your spirit.' Elijah: 'If you see me taken, you'll get it.'

They walk together, chariot of fire appears, horses of fire, Elijah taken up in whirlwind. Elisha tears his clothes, picks up Elijah's cloak, strikes Jordan River: 'Where is the Lord, God of Elijah?' Waters part. Prophets see: 'The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha.'

Elisha's miracle era begins:
- Purifies Jericho's water with salt
- Bears maul youths who mock his baldness (42 die—harsh but shows disrespect to God's prophet has consequences)
- Provides oil for widow to pay debts
- Raises Shunammite woman's son from dead
- Purifies poisoned stew
- Feeds 100 with 20 loaves
- Heals Naaman's leprosy (Syrian commander dips in Jordan 7 times after initial pride)
- Makes ax head float
- Opens servant's eyes to see fiery chariots protecting them

Meanwhile, kings continue cycling: Northern Israel has occasional moments (Jehu's purge of Ahab's house) but mostly evil. Southern Judah has occasional good kings (Hezekiah, Josiah) mixed with terrible ones.

Major northern events:
- Jehu's violent coup: kills Joram, Ahaziah, Jezebel (thrown from window, dogs eat her), Ahab's 70 sons, Baal worshippers. But continues Jeroboam's calf worship.
- Israel's final decline: Assyria rises, captures northern cities.
- 722 BC: Assyria besieges Samaria for 3 years, takes Israel captive, scatters 10 tribes—Northern Kingdom gone forever.

Southern Judah events:
- Hezekiah's reign (ch 18-20): destroys high places, smashes bronze snake Moses made (became idol). Assyria attacks, taunts: 'Don't let Hezekiah deceive you—no god can deliver from Assyrian king!' Hezekiah prays, Isaiah prophesies deliverance. Angel kills 185,000 Assyrians overnight. Hezekiah gets sick, prays, God adds 15 years. Shows Babylonian envoys all treasures—Isaiah prophesies future exile to Babylon.
- Manasseh (ch 21): Hezekiah's son, most evil Judah king. Rebuilds high places, practices sorcery, consults mediums, sacrifices son in fire, fills Jerusalem with innocent blood. God decrees Judah's exile because of him.
- Josiah (ch 22-23): 8-year-old king, finds Book of Law in temple during repairs. Tearing clothes, consults prophetess Huldah. She says judgment coming but delayed because of his repentance. Josiah launches radical reform: destroys pagan altars, removes idolatrous priests, celebrates Passover like never since judges. Dies in battle against Egypt.

Last chapters: Judah's final kings rebel against Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem, takes treasures, exiles people including King Jehoiachin.

Zedekiah rebels, Babylon returns, destroys temple, breaches walls, burns city, exiles most remaining people. Only poor left to work vineyards. Governor Gedaliah assassinated, remaining Jews flee to Egypt.

Book ends with exiled king Jehoiachin released from prison in Babylon after 37 years, given seat above other kings—tiny hope flicker.
outro:
2 Kings concludes with both kingdoms in ruins: Israel exiled to Assyria (722 BC), Judah to Babylon (586 BC). The temple—Solomon's magnificent center of worship—is burned rubble. Davidic dynasty appears ended.

Why did this happen? The narrator makes it clear: persistent idolatry, rejection of prophets, violation of covenant. Even good kings like Hezekiah and Josiah couldn't undo centuries of accumulated sin (especially Manasseh's).

Key patterns:
1. **Prophetic faithfulness** – Elijah/Elisha miracles show God's power even when kings reject Him.
2. **The 'yet' moments** – God delays judgment multiple times because of repentant kings' prayers.
3. **Foreign policy failures** – Kings constantly trust alliances (Egypt, Assyria) over God.
4. **Covenant consequences** – Deuteronomy's blessings/curses play out exactly as warned.

But hope remains in small gestures: Naaman's healing shows God cares for Gentiles. Josiah's reform shows repentance matters. Jehoiachin's release hints Davidic line isn't dead.

Historically, the exile becomes refining fire: Israel loses land, temple, monarchy—everything they thought defined them—and must learn: God is enough without those things.

This ends the 'Deuteronomistic History' (Joshua–2 Kings). The next historical books (Chronicles) will retell this story from priestly perspective with different emphases.

The stage is set for prophets who ministered during this period (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel) and the post-exile books (Ezra, Nehemiah). God's story isn't over.
